reasons: The source explicitly says it is important to align with the demographic and describes Boom as a pro-age brand for an older demographic.
The described mega-menu actions and revenue outcome are supported.

The trigger overstates the source: the source says that, in session recordings, most new visitors who are directed to a homepage or store page click the mega menu. The candidate omits both the 'most' qualifier and the directed-to-page condition.
The source explicitly says Boom customers were surveyed and that the survey informed the PDP updates.
The listed PDP changes—higher reviews/social proof, visible savings, sticky add to cart, gallery thumbnails, and guarantee prominence—are all described in the source.
The dependency on customer survey findings is supported because the source says the survey informed these PDP updates.
The source describes making the money-back-guarantee information readily visible by the call to action and reports that more people purchased.
The source specifically frames the concern as relevant to Boom's older target demographic; the candidate preserves that trigger.
The source explicitly advises treating an existing image carousel as a mini landing page, adding the listed content types and seals, and using thumbnails rather than radial dots.
The trigger and exclusion accurately retain the condition that an image carousel is present and the instruction not to use radial dots.
The candidate accurately reports the source's assertion that more people will fully go through an image carousel than the whole page.
The source expressly recommends removing a discount box from the cart or coupon page when the site has no active discounts.
The candidate retains the material prerequisite that no active discounts are offered.
The quoted coupon-search and abandonment rationale is present in the source.

However, the source gives this rationale in the context of sites without active discounts. The candidate's trigger is merely that a discount box is present, making the warning appear to apply even where active discounts are available.
The source explicitly describes adding a cart trust-policy bar and lists easy returns, support, satisfaction guarantee, and money-back guarantee as its contents.
The action and exception are supported: the source says to use labels such as bestsellers and new on only a couple of side-by-side products, not every product.
The stated dependency on the collection-page principle is unsupported and too narrow. The source explicitly says this labeling can also be used on homepages and 'often bought with' sections.
The source supports the case-specific action of showing prices on collection-page buttons for Boom's consumable, repeat-purchase product and says it did not work for every product or niche.
The dependency on the general collection-page showcase/filter principle is not stated as a prerequisite for pricing buttons.
The stated exclusion is non-operational: the source does not identify which products or niches are unsuitable, only that the approach does not work universally.
The source explicitly calls for a 2x2 presentation and four products above the fold on mobile, and warns against large heroes or text blocks when they prevent products from appearing above the fold.
The dependency on the separate general collection-page principle is not stated as a prerequisite; it is an additional rule in the same discussion rather than a required prior action.
The stated principle is supported by the source's collection-page advice.
The dependency on the separate showcase-and-filter principle is not established as a prerequisite in the source.

The source describes all listed landing-page changes for Boom's older audience, including demographic-matched imagery, larger fonts, scannable copy, value-driven headline, bullets, bolded headings, and an easy-to-understand buy box.
The source explicitly says collection pages should showcase products and enable easy filtering.
The source says that most new visitors directed to a homepage or store page will click the mega menu to see products, categories, and available options.
The candidate retains the relevant page-direction condition and notes the lack of methodology details.
The candidate accurately presents this as the speaker's characterization of the previous, typical default-Shopify-style design, rather than as a measured click-through result.
The source explicitly states the herd-mentality rationale and the recommendation to give people a reason to click.
The source reports nearly $50,000 in incremental monthly revenue for the mega-menu test.
The dependency on the separate claim about new visitors using mega menus is not established as a necessary prerequisite for the reported result; it is part of the presenter’s rationale for the test.
Immediately after describing the money-back-guarantee test, the source reports 'Again, nearly $40,000.' The candidate appropriately notes that currency and period are not supplied.
The source explicitly reports an extra 50 cents for each person sent to the PDP through paid media.
The source reports $40,000 in monthly revenue for the cart optimization.

It does not attribute that result to the trust-policy bar alone: the cart optimization included both removing the discount box and adding the trust-policy bar. The title therefore over-attributes the reported outcome.
The source reports 30K in monthly revenue from the two combined collection-page changes: labels and price display.
The source explicitly asserts that workshop participants under 300,000 sessions would receive the biggest uplift from pages like the example.
The candidate correctly records that the excerpt supplies neither the threshold's time period nor its basis.
The source describes a page as 'five makeup tips for older women' in a listicle style, but does not explicitly identify this phrase as the page title.
Revise the claim to say the landing page used that listicle concept rather than asserting a confirmed title.
The candidate accurately reproduces the source's instruction that visitors should understand what is being sold and the benefit as easily as a five-year-old would.
The source says the page 'crushed it' on cold traffic, produced 20k per month, and allowed scaling.
The candidate appropriately identifies missing currency and traffic-source details.
The excerpt states that 13 tests out of 135 won and visibly cuts off immediately afterward. The candidate does not infer a missing conclusion.
The source supports using data to hypothesize and create a test variation.

The prerequisite is circular: it says data must already have been used to form the hypothesis for the action of using data to form a hypothesis. It should instead state an available-data input, or omit the prerequisite.
The source defines these as non-money links, gives contact, reviews, and FAQs as examples, and instructs that they be pushed to the bottom as secondary to products.
The source says people were 'fomoing into a product' after the bestseller carousel showed that others were buying.
The candidate changes this to a claim that the carousel makes more people buy. The excerpt does not explicitly establish purchase rather than interest, clicking, or product selection.
The source explicitly says new customers need to be nudged in a certain direction in the mega-menu discussion.
The source literally says the box was collapsed and that the information was readily available near the CTA.
The candidate properly flags that the surrounding transcript is internally unclear about the prior collapsed state and does not invent the visual details.
The source characterizes the discount-box experience as especially poor for the older demographic, within the condition that the site has no active discounts.
The candidate acknowledges that universal applicability to all older audiences is not established.
The source explicitly says that the trust-policy bar provides positive reaffirmation that the business is a real brand when customers reach the cart.

The source explicitly extends the labeling advice to any side-by-side products, including homepages, often-bought-with sections, and collection pages, while saying only a couple should stand out and not every product should be labeled.

omissions.description: For the cited consumable-product use case, the source specifically advises enabling direct add-to-cart from the collection page after showing the price, rather than requiring the product-details path. The price-display candidate only says this reduces steps and does not represent the direct collection-page add-to-cart action.
omissions.quote: Just go to a collection page. You see the price. you add it to the cart from the collection.

source_limitations: The excerpt begins mid-sentence and ends mid-sentence, so surrounding context is missing rather than demonstrably erroneous.
It is a noisy spoken transcript with ambiguous or contradictory wording, notably around whether the money-back-guarantee box was previously collapsed.

Revenue and uplift figures are presenter-reported; the excerpt supplies no experiment design, control/variant details, sample sizes, statistical results, attribution method, currency, or consistent reporting period.
Several behavioral and demographic statements are asserted without an underlying measurement method or evidence in the excerpt.
The 300,000-session threshold has no stated time window, basis, or definition of session scope.
